analysis.one_liner: Exempts every business operating in Ohio from all federal laws and regulations.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee and subcommittee, never received a vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. James Traficant's bill would have exempted any person operating a trade or business in Ohio from every federal law and regulation that applies to such a business. Taken literally, that would wipe out federal workplace safety rules, minimum wage and overtime requirements, environmental protections, consumer protections, and tax obligations for Ohio businesses, while leaving competing businesses in other states fully subject to those same laws. The bill was referred to the House Government Operations Committee and its Subcommittee on Legislation and National Security, and it never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Ohio businesses would be freed from every federal requirement touching their operations — compliance costs, safety rules, wage and hour standards, environmental limits, and federal taxes and penalties tied to the business. Ohio workers, consumers, and the air and water federal law protects would lose those protections at any business claiming the exemption.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ohio businesses exempt from federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Any person operating a trade or business in Ohio would be exempt from all federal laws and regulations applying to that trade or business, removing federal compliance burdens entirely for those businesses.

analysis.who_pays: Ohio workers would lose federal workplace protections such as safety standards and wage and hour rules at exempt businesses; consumers and residents would lose federal consumer, environmental, and health protections tied to those businesses; and businesses in other states would keep paying the costs Ohio businesses shed, competing on unequal terms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ohio workers, consumers, and competing businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill as written would eliminate federal workplace safety, wage, consumer, and environmental protections for anyone operating a business in Ohio, leaving those workers and residents without federal legal remedies.

It would treat Ohio businesses differently from identical businesses in every other state, inviting a constitutional conflict over whether Congress can selectively nullify federal law for one state's businesses.
The bill contained no enforcement mechanism, no implementation details, and no limits, making it unworkable as drafted even for supporters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered Ohio businesses relief from federal compliance costs, but at the cost of stripping federal safety, wage, consumer, and environmental protections from Ohio workers and residents, and putting Ohio businesses on a different legal footing than their competitors elsewhere. Even its single cosponsor's support did not produce any committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Government Operations Committee and a subcommittee from April 1992 until the Congress ended in January 1993, and no vote was ever held on it.

narrative.text: Rep. James Traficant introduced the bill on April 28, 1992, to exempt any person operating a trade or business in Ohio from all federal laws and regulations applying to such a business.
The House referred it to the Committee on Government Operations on April 28, 1992.
Two days later, on April 30, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Legislation and National Security, where it remained with no further action.
The bill had one Democratic cosponsor and never received a vote or any committee consideration beyond referral before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ohio workers, consumers, and residents were better off because the bill never advanced — federal workplace, consumer, and environmental protections continued to apply to Ohio businesses. Businesses in other states also avoided competing against Ohio firms exempt from federal law.

for.name: Rep. James A. Traficant, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt all Ohio businesses from every federal law and regulation applying to them.

against.name: House Committee on Government Operations
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Legislation and National Security and never reported it back or scheduled any consideration.

sides.party_line_note: With one sponsor, one Democratic cosponsor, and no votes or recorded opposition, the bill never generated a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have freed every Ohio business from federal laws covering its operations, including wage, safety, consumer, environmental, and tax obligations. The gain for those businesses comes directly at the cost of protections for Ohio workers, consumers, and residents.

industries.industry: Businesses in other states competing with Ohio firms
industries.note: They would have remained subject to all federal rules while Ohio competitors shed those costs, putting them at a competitive disadvantage. Consumers elsewhere would not directly benefit from that imbalance.
Every federal agency's authority over Ohio businesses — workplace safety inspections, environmental enforcement, wage and hour compliance — would have been nullified by the exemption.
